title: Seeking a Trippy Placebo - Nautilus
gist: Psychedelic drug trials struggle to blind participants because patients can tell drug from placebo, which may inflate apparent efficacy. Meanwhile, US policy is accelerating: a presidential executive order fast-tracks psychedelic approvals and the FDA has held a public hearing.

insights.claim: Psychedelics distort perception so strongly that placebo-controlled trials are hard to blind, because patients usually work out whether they received drug or placebo.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Blinding failure is a key regulatory and efficacy risk for psychedelic drug developers; watch trial designs that use active placebos.
insights.locator: The psychedelic renaissance has a problem

insights.claim: Unblinding on both sides may exaggerate therapeutic differences and make psychedelics look more effective in trials than they really are.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Reported effect sizes for psychedelic therapies may shrink under better blinding, which is a downside risk for valuations built on trial data.
insights.quote: making psychedelics appear more effective than they really are in clinical trial results

insights.claim: A presidential executive order at the start of the year directed federal agencies to speed up research, review, and approval of psychedelic therapies for serious mental illnesses, including depression, anxiety, and addiction.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: This policy tailwind for psychedelic therapeutics could shorten approval timelines.

insights.speaker: Kristen French

insights.claim: Demand for psychedelic medicines in the United States is growing at the same time as the methodological problems in their trials remain unresolved.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Policy momentum is running ahead of evidence quality, which creates a risk of later reversals or safety-driven setbacks.
